Sending money abroad: chart the exchange-rate markup as well as the transfer fee

Read a dated official transfer-cost case, then compare hypothetical services on the CAD required to deliver the same net foreign-currency amount.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare the CAD needed to deliver the same net foreign-currency amount

Interactive planning lab

Service A: CAD needed for the budget period$17,304
Service B: CAD needed for the budget period$17,004
CAD saved using B instead of A; negative means dearer$300

One fixed official case chart is separate from the editable hypothetical model. The model uses generic foreign-currency units (FCU), not a live currency quote. A markup increases a reference CAD-per-FCU rate. The sender funds a common recipient charge so both services deliver the selected net amount. Sender fees are additional CAD charges. All transfers repeat identical inputs with no rate movement, taxes, funding charges or delivery delay. A zero net target means no transfer and no charge.

On this page

  1. Give the recipient the same net amount in both comparisons
  2. Read the official case as dated evidence with a limited scope

The central idea

Compare the amount the recipient actually receives with the complete CAD payment. A zero sender fee can still accompany a less favourable conversion rate.

01

Give the recipient the same net amount in both comparisons

An international transfer has two sides: what leaves the sender’s account and what becomes available to the recipient. Comparing sender fees alone can miss a difference in the exchange rate or a charge deducted at the other end.

The FCAC’s money-transfer guidance recommends considering transfer charges, exchange-rate costs and possible recipient charges. It also identifies delivery timing as part of a service comparison. This article’s editable model isolates the amount calculation and does not evaluate a provider’s reliability, speed or protections.

The model fixes the recipient’s net need, expressed in generic foreign-currency units, or FCU. Both hypothetical services must deliver that same amount after a common recipient charge. The sender supplies enough additional foreign currency to cover that charge. This creates a comparison with the same final benefit instead of comparing two transfers that leave different amounts available abroad.

02

Read the official case as dated evidence with a limited scope

The fixed chart reproduces the fee and conversion-markup components from FCAC’s published worked example. Its three anonymized services deliver USD 1,000 using quotes recorded on 23 June 2026. The page is dated 23 October 2026.

Those are selected case quotes, not a representative distribution or present-day provider ranking. The chart remains fixed when model controls change. Its role is to show two separate cost components; the editable comparison below uses different, explicitly invented terms.

For the model, retain that habit of separating components, then obtain supported quotes for the actual transaction. A quote needs a date, a currency pair, the amount sent, the net receipt and the funding method. Comparing figures from different times or payment methods can introduce another difference that the fee label does not explain.

03

State which currency is on each side of the exchange rate

The selected reference rate is 1.40 CAD per FCU. At that rate, delivering 1,000 FCU without any charges has a reference principal of CAD 1,400. The reference is hypothetical; it is not a live market rate, a guaranteed executable rate or the historical rate used in the official case.

A markup is added to this CAD-per-FCU rate. Service A’s assumed 3% markup produces 1.40 × 1.03 = 1.442 CAD per FCU. Service B’s 0.5% markup produces 1.407 CAD per FCU. A larger number in this quotation direction means more Canadian dollars are required for each foreign-currency unit.

Reversing the quotation to FCU per CAD would reverse that visual direction. Taking the reciprocal changes the rate’s units, and an apparently identical percentage adjustment would not necessarily describe the same conversion. The calculator keeps one explicit CAD-per-FCU convention throughout rather than mixing quotation directions across the charts.

04

Reconcile the complete payment and repeated budget

At the default 1,000 FCU net receipt and zero recipient fee, Service A requires CAD 1,442 and charges no separate sender fee. The extra cost above the CAD 1,400 reference principal is CAD 42 per transfer.

Service B requires CAD 1,407 for the conversion plus a CAD 10 sender fee, for a total of CAD 1,417. Its extra cost is CAD 17 per transfer. Its nonzero visible fee is compatible with a CAD 25 lower total payment under these invented terms.

Twelve identical transfers require CAD 17,304 through A and CAD 17,004 through B, a CAD 300 difference. These are full CAD funding budgets, including money delivered for the recipient’s use. They are not entirely fees. The group bars place reference principal beside total payment so that the principal and the extra costs are not confused.

05

Test transfer size and recipient charges separately

The extra-cost curve varies only the net foreign-currency receipt per transfer. A flat sender fee has more weight relative to a small transfer, while a rate markup grows with the converted amount. Their combination can make the preferred cost result depend on transfer size.

With the default terms and no recipient charge, the difference between the two modeled rate markups is 2.5% of the CAD 1.40 reference rate, or CAD 0.035 per FCU. Offsetting B’s extra CAD 10 sender fee therefore requires about 285.71 FCU per transfer. This is a threshold for the invented quotes, rather than a general minimum remittance amount.

A recipient charge changes the foreign-currency amount that must be purchased. For example, a 20 FCU deduction means funding 1,020 FCU to leave 1,000 FCU net. The model applies the service’s rate to the full 1,020 FCU. At a zero net target, it assumes no transfer at all and charges nothing, so the flat-fee curve has a separate zero-transfer boundary.

06

Use the matrix to prepare a quote comparison

The matrix varies the net receipt and Service B’s rate markup. Other selected terms stay fixed, including sender fees, the recipient charge, reference rate and transfer count. Positive cells mean B costs less over the budget period; negative cells mean A costs less.

All repeated transfers use identical inputs. The model does not predict exchange rates over a year or assume that today’s quote will remain available. If future receipts are needed on several dates, record those deadlines and stress the reference rate separately. A lower fee does not remove the risk of an adverse currency movement before a later transfer.

For an actual payment, confirm how the transfer will be funded, when the rate is fixed, what the recipient can collect and how completion is confirmed. Include any additional funding or intermediary charges that apply. Keep the receipt and reference number. The graphs explain the amount comparison, while the actual payment plan also needs supported terms and enough time for the money to arrive.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The fixed FCAC chart is an official worked example using quotes recorded on 23 June 2026, not representative statistics or current offers. The other three charts are hypothetical models in generic foreign-currency units. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
